label: High-Dimensional Asymptotics
notes: This chapter studies what happens to statistics on Stiefel and Grassmann manifolds when the ambient dimension grows without bound. We frame the central theme up front: geometry that feels exotic in low dimensions becomes rigid and predictable as dimension increases, and that rigidity is exactly what makes asymptotic inference tractable for practitioners.

label: The Growing-Dimension Regime
notes: Here we fix the bookkeeping for the whole deck. The ambient dimension m grows, the frame size p may stay fixed or grow with m, and every limiting statement is read against that ratio. Students should leave this slide knowing which quantity is held constant and which is sent to infinity throughout.

label: Concentration of Measure on Spheres
notes: The first phenomenon is concentration of measure. On a high-dimensional sphere almost all surface area sits in a thin band near any equator. We give the exponential tail bound and stress that the width of that band shrinks like one over the square root of the dimension, which drives everything later in the chapter.

label: Levy's Lemma and Lipschitz Statistics
notes: Levy's lemma upgrades concentration of area into concentration of functions. Any Lipschitz statistic on the sphere clusters tightly around its mean with Gaussian tails. We connect this directly to estimators on the Stiefel manifold, since smooth functionals of a random frame inherit the same sharp concentration behavior in growing dimension.

label: Near-Orthogonality of Random Frames
notes: This slide makes precise the slogan that random high-dimensional vectors are nearly orthogonal. The inner product of two independent uniform unit vectors concentrates at zero with standard deviation one over the square root of the dimension, so a sampled frame behaves like an exactly orthonormal one as m grows large.

label: Inner Products Concentrate at Zero
notes: We quantify the previous slogan with a distribution. The scaled inner product of two uniform unit vectors is asymptotically standard normal, and its histogram collapses onto a spike at the origin as dimension climbs. This is the engine behind Johnson-Lindenstrauss style preservation of geometry under random projection.

label: Limiting Law of the Largest Coordinate
notes: A uniform point on a high-dimensional sphere has coordinates that are jointly close to independent Gaussians after scaling. We use this to describe extreme-value behavior of the largest coordinate and to caution that maxima grow only like the square root of a logarithm of the dimension, which is remarkably slow.

label: Stiefel and Grassmann as m Grows
notes: Now we lift single-vector facts to frames and subspaces. Columns of a uniform Stiefel matrix become asymptotically independent Gaussian directions, and a uniform Grassmann subspace looks like the span of such directions. The fixed-p, growing-m regime is where these clean Gaussian surrogates become exact in the limit.

label: Principal Angles Between Random Subspaces
notes: Two independent uniform subspaces meet at principal angles whose cosines concentrate near zero as dimension grows, so random subspaces are almost orthogonal complements. We give the leading-order law of these cosines and tie it back to near-orthogonality of the underlying frames from the earlier slides.

label: Gaussian Surrogate and CLT
notes: This slide states the central-limit backbone. Smooth statistics of a uniform frame, once centered and scaled by the square root of the dimension, converge to Gaussian limits whose covariance we can compute from the tangent space. This is the asymptotic distribution result that powers tests and confidence regions on the manifold.

label: Worked Estimate: Frame Coherence
notes: We run a concrete calculation. The mutual coherence of a random frame, the largest off-diagonal inner product magnitude, is bounded with high probability by a square-root-log-over-dimension rate. Students see the union bound and the Gaussian tail combine into a usable finite-sample guarantee for sampled high-dimensional frames.

label: Pitfalls and Recap
notes: We close by naming traps: intuition from three dimensions misleads, fixed thresholds become meaningless, and the ratio of frame size to ambient dimension must be tracked. The recap reassembles concentration, near-orthogonality, and the Gaussian limit into one coherent toolkit for high-dimensional manifold statistics and asymptotic inference.
